```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The nine tasks</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Answer each task on paper first, then open its worked solution. Task 9 is the main estimate; its worked solution and the rubric are further down this page.</p>
<ol class="ckf-static">
<li><p><b>Why balance every moment?</b> <span class="lx-hint">Explain a mechanism · draws on T0, T3</span></p><p>In one or two sentences: why must supply equal demand at every moment on a power grid, and what tells the operator when it does not?</p><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 1</summary><p>Power is made as it is used; spinning machines' <span class="lx-term" data-term="inertia">inertia</span>, or a fast reserve such as a battery, bridges a gap only briefly. A shortfall lowers the <span class="lx-term" data-term="frequency">frequency</span>, a surplus raises it, and controls restore the balance and 60 Hz.</p><p>A full answer makes two points:</p><ul><li>The grid stores little energy, so power is made as it is used; stored energy, in spinning machines' inertia or a fast reserve such as a battery, bridges a gap only until controls act.</li><li>The frequency shows a gap: a shortfall makes it fall below 60 Hz and a surplus makes it rise; controls then restore the balance and bring it back to 60 Hz.</li></ul></details></li>
<li><p><b>Phone charges in a day</b> <span class="lx-hint">Estimate with units · draws on T1</span></p><p>A U.S. home buys about 10,800 kWh of electricity a year. A phone takes about 15 Wh for a full charge (illustrative). About how many full charges equal one day of those purchases?</p><ul><li>a. 2</li><li>b. 80</li><li>c. 2,000</li><li>d. 720,000</li></ul><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 2</summary><p><b>Answer: c. 2,000.</b></p><p>One day: 10,800 kWh ÷ 365 ≈ 30 kWh = 30,000 Wh, and 30,000 Wh ÷ 15 Wh ≈ 2,000 charges. The trap is the k: kWh and Wh differ by a factor of 1,000.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A December day's demand</b> <span class="lx-hint">Read a chart · draws on T2</span></p><p>The chart shows Prairie Town's demand on a real December weekday. When is demand highest, and how much above the day's lowest hour?</p><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Chart data: Monday 15 December 2025, MW by hour</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Hour</th><th scope="col">Demand (MW)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>00:00</td><td>306</td></tr><tr><td>01:00</td><td>304</td></tr><tr><td>02:00</td><td>304</td></tr><tr><td>03:00</td><td>306</td></tr><tr><td>04:00</td><td>311</td></tr><tr><td>05:00</td><td>321</td></tr><tr><td>06:00</td><td>338</td></tr><tr><td>07:00</td><td>347</td></tr><tr><td>08:00</td><td>344</td></tr><tr><td>09:00</td><td>335</td></tr><tr><td>10:00</td><td>326</td></tr><tr><td>11:00</td><td>318</td></tr><tr><td>12:00</td><td>311</td></tr><tr><td>13:00</td><td>288</td></tr><tr><td>14:00</td><td>282</td></tr><tr><td>15:00</td><td>282</td></tr><tr><td>16:00</td><td>286</td></tr><tr><td>17:00</td><td>296</td></tr><tr><td>18:00</td><td>301</td></tr><tr><td>19:00</td><td>303</td></tr><tr><td>20:00</td><td>303</td></tr><tr><td>21:00</td><td>302</td></tr><tr><td>22:00</td><td>294</td></tr><tr><td>23:00</td><td>287</td></tr></tbody></table></div></details><ul><li>a. 07:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour</li><li>b. 07:00, about 4 times the lowest hour</li><li>c. 19:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour</li><li>d. 14:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour</li></ul><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 3</summary><p><b>Answer: a. 07:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour.</b></p><p>Peak 347 MW at 07:00, low 282 MW at 14:00 and 15:00: 347 ÷ 282 ≈ 1.23, about a quarter higher. Always read where the axis starts, here at 260 MW, not zero.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>After a plant trips</b> <span class="lx-hint">Explain a mechanism · draws on T3</span></p><p>A 60 MW gas unit in Prairie Town's region trips (shuts down suddenly). Put what happens next in order, first at the top.</p><p>As shuffled:</p><ul><li>Within minutes, the operator's control system orders reserve plants (spare capacity kept ready) up to replace the lost 60 MW.</li><li>The frequency starts to fall below 60 Hz; the spinning machines' stored energy covers the gap for a moment.</li><li>The frequency is back at 60 Hz, and the operator restores its reserves for the next trip.</li><li>Within seconds, governors (automatic speed controls on running plants) raise output and the fall stops.</li></ul><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 4</summary><ol><li>The frequency starts to fall below 60 Hz; the spinning machines' stored energy covers the gap for a moment.</li><li>Within seconds, governors (automatic speed controls on running plants) raise output and the fall stops.</li><li>Within minutes, the operator's control system orders reserve plants (spare capacity kept ready) up to replace the lost 60 MW.</li><li>The frequency is back at 60 Hz, and the operator restores its reserves for the next trip.</li></ol><p>The frequency falls first; governors stop the fall within seconds but leave it below 60 Hz. Reserves replace the lost power over minutes and bring 60 Hz back; only then are the reserves rebuilt.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Forecast against actual</b> <span class="lx-hint">Read a chart · draws on T4</span></p><p>The chart shows the day-ahead forecast and the actual demand of a real spring day, scaled to Prairie Town. Over the day, the forecast was mostly…</p><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Chart data: Thursday 17 April 2025, MW by hour</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Hour</th><th scope="col">Actual demand (MW)</th><th scope="col">Day-ahead forecast (MW)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>00:00</td><td>228</td><td>225</td></tr><tr><td>01:00</td><td>221</td><td>220</td></tr><tr><td>02:00</td><td>217</td><td>216</td></tr><tr><td>03:00</td><td>216</td><td>215</td></tr><tr><td>04:00</td><td>216</td><td>217</td></tr><tr><td>05:00</td><td>224</td><td>225</td></tr><tr><td>06:00</td><td>238</td><td>239</td></tr><tr><td>07:00</td><td>248</td><td>248</td></tr><tr><td>08:00</td><td>253</td><td>251</td></tr><tr><td>09:00</td><td>257</td><td>254</td></tr><tr><td>10:00</td><td>263</td><td>259</td></tr><tr><td>11:00</td><td>268</td><td>264</td></tr><tr><td>12:00</td><td>275</td><td>270</td></tr><tr><td>13:00</td><td>284</td><td>278</td></tr><tr><td>14:00</td><td>290</td><td>284</td></tr><tr><td>15:00</td><td>295</td><td>290</td></tr><tr><td>16:00</td><td>299</td><td>297</td></tr><tr><td>17:00</td><td>300</td><td>298</td></tr><tr><td>18:00</td><td>298</td><td>297</td></tr><tr><td>19:00</td><td>292</td><td>291</td></tr><tr><td>20:00</td><td>288</td><td>288</td></tr><tr><td>21:00</td><td>280</td><td>279</td></tr><tr><td>22:00</td><td>266</td><td>265</td></tr><tr><td>23:00</td><td>252</td><td>250</td></tr></tbody></table></div></details><ul><li>a. too low, by at most about 2% of demand</li><li>b. too high, by at most about 2% of demand</li><li>c. too low, by up to about 20% of demand</li><li>d. exactly right</li></ul><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 5</summary><p><b>Answer: a. too low, by at most about 2% of demand.</b></p><p>Actual demand is above the forecast in 19 of 24 hours; the largest miss is 6 MW at 13:00 and 14:00, about 2% of demand. Operators hold reserves to cover misses like these.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A wind farm's year</b> <span class="lx-hint">Estimate with units · draws on T5</span></p><p>A 50 MW wind farm runs at the 2025 U.S. average capacity factor for wind, 33.8%. About how much energy does it make in a year?</p><p>Answer with a number and a unit.</p><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 6</summary><p><b>Answer: about 148 GWh.</b></p><p>50 MW × 8,760 h × 0.338 ≈ 148,000 MWh, or 148 GWh. Without the <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span> you would get 438,000 MWh: the farm at full output every hour, which no wind farm does.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>A windless winter evening</b> <span class="lx-hint">Explain a mechanism · draws on T6</span></p><p>A windless winter evening at 18:00, with demand near its peak. Assume every plant is available and has fuel. Which pair can Prairie Town count on?</p><ul><li>a. The solar farm and the wind farm</li><li>b. The gas peaker and the nuclear plant</li><li>c. The wind farm and the nuclear plant</li><li>d. Rooftop solar and the gas peaker</li></ul><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 7</summary><p><b>Answer: b. The gas peaker and the nuclear plant.</b></p><p><span class="lx-term" data-term="firm-capacity">Firm capacity</span> is output you can count on when it is needed. At a calm winter dusk, with plants available and fuelled, that is the gas <span class="lx-term" data-term="peaker">peaker</span> and the nuclear plant; wind and solar do other jobs.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>Spot the error in a headline</b> <span class="lx-hint">Spot an error · draws on N1</span></p><p>Made-up headline: “New 100 MW solar farm will power 100,000 homes.” At the 2025 U.S. solar capacity factor (24.0%) and 10,800 kWh bought per home a year, about how many homes' yearly purchases does it equal?</p><ul><li>a. 4,000</li><li>b. 20,000</li><li>c. 100,000</li><li>d. 200,000</li></ul><details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Worked solution, task 8</summary><p><b>Answer: b. 20,000.</b></p><p>100 MW × 8,760 h × 0.240 ≈ 210,000 MWh a year, or about 19,500 homes' yearly purchases at 10.8 MWh each. Even nameplate (maximum rated) output every hour would equal only about 81,000: the headline fails the physics question.</p></details></li>
<li><p><b>The school-bus estimate</b> <span class="lx-hint">Estimate (main task) · draws on T1, T5, N1</span></p><p>Prairie Town's 20 diesel school buses go electric. Estimate the electricity they will use in a year, stating your assumptions. The fields below ask for a range with units, the main uncertainty and one way to check.</p><p>On paper: a low and a high value with units, your inputs and steps, the main uncertainty and one way to check.</p></li>
</ol>
```

## Worked solution: the school-bus estimate
:::

```{=html}
<div id="ckf-lock" class="lx-ck-lock" hidden>
<p><b>Opens when you submit task 9.</b> The checkpoint asks for an estimate without hints, so the worked solution waits for your own numbers.</p>
<p><button type="button" class="lx-btn ghost small">Open it anyway (recorded)</button></p>
</div>
<div id="ckf-solution-body" class="lx-xgrid lx-ck-gated">
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Two routes to the mileage, one range for energy per mile</h3></header>
<table class="lx-facts ckf-routes">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Step</th><th scope="col">Route A: per school day</th><th scope="col">Route B: per year</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Miles</td><td>20 buses × 50 miles a day (a 25-mile morning and a 25-mile afternoon route) × 180 school days (assumed) = 180,000 miles</td><td>20 buses × 14,084 miles a year (U.S. average for a school bus) = 281,680 miles</td></tr>
<tr><td>Energy per mile</td><td colspan="2">1.3 kWh per mile (large buses as rated by makers, 1.26–1.58) to 2.3 kWh per mile (a planning worst case: cold, heating, hills)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Year</td><td class="n">234,000 to 414,000 kWh: about 230 to 410 MWh</td><td class="n">366,000 to 648,000 kWh: about 370 to 650 MWh</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul class="ckf-list">
<li><b>Answer:</b> about 230 to 650 MWh a year, near 440 MWh in the middle.</li>
<li><b>Mileage boundary:</b> Route A counts school runs only, not field trips, sports or summer use, so it runs low.</li>
<li><b>Electricity boundary:</b> energy at the bus; charging losses add a little more at the meter.</li>
<li><b>Shared input:</b> both routes use the same energy per mile, so their overlap does not check it.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Uncertainty and checks</h3></header>
<ul class="ckf-list">
<li><b>Main uncertainty: energy per mile.</b> It spans nearly a factor of two, from 1.3 to 2.3 kWh per mile, with cold weather and cabin heat at the high end.</li>
<li><b>Next: miles per bus.</b> Route B's 14,084 miles is about 1.6 times Route A's 9,000.</li>
<li><b>Scale, not a check: homes.</b> 440 MWh = 440,000 kWh; 440,000 ÷ 10,791 kWh per home ≈ 41 average U.S. homes' yearly electricity purchases.</li>
<li><b>Scale, not a check: the town.</b> Prairie Town uses about 2,470 GWh a year, so the buses add about 0.02%. A wrong estimate converts just as neatly, so neither comparison tests it.</li>
<li><b>Plausibility: a day's energy.</b> 50 miles × 2.3 kWh per mile = 115 kWh per bus per day, within the battery sizes in EPA's October 2024 webinar (under 100 to over 300 kWh).</li>
<li><b>Its limit.</b> A real bus needs that much usable energy, plus a reserve, so a small battery may not cover the worst day.</li>
<li><b>Check with records.</b> The district's yearly mileage replaces Route B's national average. A comparable electric fleet's measured charging energy also checks the energy per mile, the input both routes share.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>The bus numbers and their sources</h3></header>
<div class="lx-scroll-x">
<table class="lx-facts">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Number</th><th scope="col">What it means</th><th scope="col">Source</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td class="n">14,084 miles</td><td>Average miles a U.S. school bus travels in a year.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://afdc.energy.gov/data/10309">U.S. DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center</a> · accessed 2 Nov 2026</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">1.26–1.58 and 2.3 kWh/mile</td><td>Energy per mile of large electric school buses as rated by makers, and a planning worst case.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/csb-fleet-plan-rte-analysis-webinar-2024-10-08.pdf">EPA Clean School Bus webinar</a> (PDF), slides 21–25 · 8 Oct 2024</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">under 100 to over 300 kWh</td><td>Battery sizes of electric school buses; usable energy is less, after wear and a minimum charge.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/csb-fleet-plan-rte-analysis-webinar-2024-10-08.pdf">EPA Clean School Bus webinar</a> (PDF), slides 16 and 26 · 8 Oct 2024</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>Marking guide in one line each</h3></header>
<ul class="ckf-list">
<li><b>Units:</b> energy per year (kWh, MWh or GWh a year), never kW or MW.</li>
<li><b>Range:</b> a low and a high from stated inputs (buses, miles, kWh per mile) that meets 230–650 MWh a year, or argues for a different one.</li>
<li><b>Uncertainty:</b> names the input that moves the answer most, and why.</li>
<li><b>Check:</b> one check that brings in an independent input (a record or a measured fleet), not “look it up”. A comparison with homes or the town gives scale, not a check.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
```

## Rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>The estimate, criterion by criterion</h3></header>
<div class="lx-scroll-x">
<table id="ckf-rubric" class="lx-facts">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Criterion</th><th scope="col">Not yet</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr data-c="units"><th scope="row">Units</th><td data-l="Not yet">A unit of power (kW, MW), or none.</td><td data-l="Developing">Energy, but no time basis, or units mixed in the steps.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Energy per year, with every conversion right.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also put in a familiar comparison: homes, or a share of the town.</td></tr>
<tr data-c="range"><th scope="row">Range and reasoning</th><td data-l="Not yet">One number, or more than ten times off the worked solution's range.</td><td data-l="Developing">A range without stated inputs, or far from the worked solution's range with no argument.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Low and high from stated inputs with consistent units, meeting the worked solution's range or arguing for another.</td><td data-l="Strong">Two routes that differ in at least one main input and agree within their ranges.</td></tr>
<tr data-c="uncertainty"><th scope="row">Main uncertainty</th><td data-l="Not yet">None named.</td><td data-l="Developing">A list of factors, not ranked.</td><td data-l="Proficient">The input that moves the answer most, and why.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also how far it moves the answer.</td></tr>
<tr data-c="check"><th scope="row">Check</th><td data-l="Not yet">None.</td><td data-l="Developing">“Look it up”, without saying what or where.</td><td data-l="Proficient">One concrete check with an independent input: a second route, a record or a measured fleet (a comparison with homes only gives scale).</td><td data-l="Strong">The check done, with whether it agrees.</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-xcard">
<header class="lx-x-head"><h3>The checkpoint's level</h3></header>
<ul class="ckf-list">
<li><b>Proficient:</b> at least 5 of the 7 auto-marked tasks right on the first try, Proficient or better on all four estimate criteria, and both points of task 1.</li>
<li><b>Opened early:</b> a task whose worked solution you open before answering counts as not right: no points for task 1, no self-ratings for the estimate.</li>
<li><b>Strong:</b> at least 6 of 7, Proficient or better on all four criteria with Strong on at least two, and both points of task 1.</li>
<li><b>Developing:</b> at least 3 of 7, and Developing or better on every estimate criterion.</li>
<li><b>Not yet:</b> anything else. The checkpoint shows readiness for the Analyst tier; it certifies nothing.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-hint">Task 1 and the estimate are self-rated. A teacher or mentor can rate them again with the same rubric from the copied summary.</p>
</div>
</div>
```
